source_read: PDF, version of record (Lancet Psychiatry 2015;2:233-238), pp. 233-238, all pages; text extracted with pdftotext -layout; every number checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi, Figures 1-2 and Tables 3-4 at 300 dpi. Online appendix not available (not read).

claims.note: Every Di Forti 2015 number in the statement and magnitude is as printed: daily 3.04 against never use, weekends 1.04, less than weekly 0.58 (0.25-1.32), ever use 0.93 (0.67-1.52); 410 cases and 370 controls recruited by advertisement; comparator never used; adjustment includes alcohol and other drugs (Table 3 footnote). Recomputed: the printed daily interval 1.91-7.76 contains 3.04 but is not centred on it (log-scale centre 3.85); 3.04 with p=0.020 reproduces the upper limit 7.76 exactly and gives a lower limit of about 1.19, so 1.91 looks like transposed digits (the claim is right to say 'printed'). The weekends interval 0.41-1.62 does not fit p=0.929 either (1.04 with that p implies about 0.44-2.46), and the ever-use interval implies p of about 0.73, not 0.569. 'Every day' includes 3 of 507 users who used more than four days a week; frequency is each person's most consistent lifetime pattern, recalled, not current use. 'Inpatients' fits: cases were recruited at the inpatient units.

anchors.locator: Table 3, Frequency of use rows (daily estimate repeated in Table 4, p. 237)
anchors.extracted: Adjusted ORs for first-episode psychosis against people who never used cannabis: less than once a week 0.58 (95% CI 0.25-1.32), p=0.198; at weekends 1.04 (0.41-1.62), p=0.929; every day 3.04 (1.91-7.76), p=0.020. Footnote: adjusted for age, gender, ethnic origin, number of cigarettes, alcohol units, other drugs used, education and employment status. Editors' check: daily interval not centred on 3.04 (fits p=0.020 only with a lower limit near 1.19); weekends interval does not fit p=0.929.

Ever against never use, adjusted for age, gender, ethnic origin, cigarettes, alcohol units, lifetime use of other illicit drugs, education and employment: OR 0.93 (95% CI 0.67-1.52), p=0.569, n=775 (employment missing for 5): no increased risk. Same paragraph: daily use of cannabis (and daily skunk) roughly three times the odds of never use.

anchors.locator: Table 2, Lifetime history of cannabis use and Frequency of use rows; Results, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Cases (n=410) vs controls (n=370): ever used 275 (67%) vs 232 (63%), p=0.277; less than once a week 68 (17%) vs 128 (35%); at weekends 84 (20%) vs 63 (17%); every day 123 (30%) vs 41 (11%), p<0.0001. The 3 of 507 users (0.6%) who used more than four days a week were counted as every day. (Figure 1, p. 236, sums to 125 daily cases and 59 daily controls, 16%: a second, inconsistent version.)

anchors.locator: Methods > Study design and participants, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Methods > Procedures, 2nd paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Cases: all patients aged 18-65 presenting with first-episode psychosis to the inpatient units of the South London and Maudsley NHS Trust (ICD-10 F20-F29 or F30-F33, confirmed with SCAN; organic psychosis excluded), 1 May 2005 to 31 May 2011; 606 approached, 145 (24%) refused (refusers more often men, p<0.004, and Black Caribbean or Black African, p=0.001), 461 took part, 410 (89%) with cannabis data. Controls: volunteers aged 18-65 from the area served by the same units, recruited in the same period through internet and newspaper advertisements and leaflets at train stations, shops and job centres (no mention of cannabis or drugs), excluded if positive on the Psychosis Screening Questionnaire or with a previous psychotic diagnosis; 389 recruited, 370 (95%) with cannabis data. No matching described; not randomly sampled (the Discussion, p. 237, 6th paragraph, says advertising rather than random selection might have biased the findings). Regressions used n=775, employment missing for 5 (p. 236, Results, 6th and 7th paragraphs). Frequency measure: the lifetime frequency that characterised each person's most consistent pattern of use (none; less than once a week every week; at weekends; every day), from the modified Cannabis Experience Questionnaire, added from March 2006 (earlier recruits lack detailed data).

claims.note: Not supported as worded: the adjustment set. The sentence gives one set (age, gender, ethnic origin, tobacco, alcohol, other drugs, education, employment) for 2.91, 0.83, 5.40 and 0.91. That set is printed for 2.91 and 0.83 (Table 3) and for 5.40 (Table 4), but 0.91, like the other composite-measure values in the magnitude (2.70, 1.90, 0.62, 0.49), comes only from Figure 2, whose legend lists age, gender, ethnic origin, education, employment and tobacco only (no alcohol, no other drugs); the paper prints the 5.40 with both sets. Everything else from this source checks on the rendered pages: 410 patients aged 18-65, 2005-2011, 370 controls recruited by advertisement from the same area; 53% vs 19% skunk-like and 14% vs 44% hash-like (Table 2); 2.91 (1.52-3.60) and 0.83 (0.52-1.77) against never use; 5.40 (2.80-11.30); 2.70, 1.90, 0.91, 0.62, 0.49; type self-reported as the type most used (people using both types classed by the one used most), potency assigned from police seizure data, no THC or CBD measured; recalled history; PAF 24.0% stated as assuming causality. Confirmed: controls' exposure in two versions (Table 2: skunk 70, hash 162; Figure 1: 106 and 127, both summing to 370). Confirmed: intervals that do not fit: age <15 1.55 (1.00-1.39) excludes its own estimate (p=0.048 implies about 1.00-2.39); skunk-like 2.91 (1.52-3.60), abstract 2.92 (1.52-3.45), fits p=0.001 only with an upper limit near 5.5; daily 3.04 (1.91-7.76) fits p=0.020 only with a lower limit near 1.19; weekends 1.04 (0.41-1.62) and hash-like 0.83 (0.52-1.77) do not fit p=0.929 and p=0.903; 5.40 (2.80-11.30) implies p of about 0.000002, not the printed 0.001 (text) or 0.002 (abstract). All other intervals contain their estimates. Confirmed: 24% not reproducible; the case-prevalence formula the Methods describe gives 34.9% from 218/410 and 2.91 (outside the printed 17.4-30.6), and 20.5% for daily skunk use against the printed 16.0% (14.0-20.3); only daily use (20.1% vs 19.3%) comes close.

anchors.locator: Methods > Procedures, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 236
anchors.extracted: Type of cannabis = the type each person reported using most (none; low potency, hash-type; high potency, skunk-type), so people who used both were classed by the one used most (how many is not reported); the grouping follows police seizure data for London (Potter et al., 2008) and the Home Office 2008 potency study, with details in the online appendix (not available). Composite 7-level measure from this and the frequency measure. No THC or cannabidiol measured in participants' cannabis; the Discussion cites seized London samples as higher in THC than hash with almost no cannabidiol, without percentages.

anchors.locator: Methods > Statistical analysis, 3rd paragraph; Results, 9th paragraph, p. 236; Table 4, p. 237
anchors.extracted: PAF estimated with Stata's punafcc for each cannabis variable; the Methods say it depends on exposure prevalence in cases and the OR, and that causality is not established. Reported if causality is assumed: daily use 19.3% (13.1-27.0), skunk use 24.0% (17.4-30.6; Summary 24%, 17-31), daily skunk 16.0% (14.0-20.3). Editors' calculation pc x (OR-1)/OR from Table 4's inputs: 20.1%, 34.9% and 20.5%. 24.0% would need OR about 1.82 at 53% exposure, or about 150/410 cases exposed at OR 2.91.

No data on joints or grams per day; use was reported over years, not present use, and recall bias is acknowledged.

key_findings.correction: The figures and citations are as printed, but the note's 'from the cited primary studies' is wrong for one source: reference 26, Arseneault et al. (2004), is a review ('Causal association ... examination of the evidence'), so the 8% for New Zealand is a review's figure. The other figures come from primary studies (van Os et al., 2002; Henquet et al., 2005). The replication timeline's 2004 entry should say the same.

key_findings.note: The paper hedges: cannabidiol 'might explain' the null hash result. Morgan and Curran (2008) is reference 21.

reporting_issues.note: 1.55 with p=0.048 implies about 1.00-2.39, so the upper limit 1.39 is the likelier misprint (editors' calculation).

Further detail: 3.04 with p=0.020 gives back the printed upper limit 7.76 exactly and a lower limit of about 1.19, so 1.91 is probably 1.19 with the digits swapped. 2.91 with p=0.001 and lower limit 1.52 implies an upper limit of about 5.5. 1.04 with p=0.929 implies about 0.44-2.46. Ever use 0.93 (0.67-1.52) implies p of about 0.73, not 0.569 (minor).
Also, 5.40 (2.80-11.30) implies p of about 0.000002, so neither printed p (0.001 or 0.002) fits that interval.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high: the domain judgments fit the PDF. Confounding, exposure measurement (recalled type and frequency, potency from seizure data, the Figure 1 and Table 2 conflict) and selection of controls (volunteers answering advertisements; 24% of patients refused, more often men and Black Caribbean or Black African) are all high. The irreconcilable numbers (intervals, attributable fractions, two versions of the controls' exposure) are confirmed on the printed pages.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One addition: the Research-in-context panel (p. 238) says skunk use 'appears to contribute to 24% of cases' with no causal caveat. The Summary's Interpretation (p. 233) speaks of cases attributed to cannabis without the assumption, and the Summary's Methods call the volunteer controls 'population controls'.

missed: p. 236, Table 3: probable values behind the misfitting intervals, which matter for any claim that cites them. Daily use 3.04: lower limit about 1.19 rather than 1.91 (3.04 with p=0.020 reproduces 7.76 exactly). First use before 15: upper limit about 2.39. Skunk-like 2.91: upper limit about 5.5 rather than 3.60 (Summary: 3.45). Editors' calculation from the printed estimates and p-values.

p. 236, Results, 8th paragraph; p. 233; p. 237, Table 4: the interval for daily skunk use, 5.40 (2.80-11.30), implies p of about 0.000002, so neither printed p-value (0.001 in the text, 0.002 in the Summary) fits it.

pp. 235-236, Results, 6th paragraph: the text says people who used skunk every day had roughly three times the odds and cites Table 3. Table 3 has no daily-skunk row: its skunk-like 2.91 covers any frequency, and daily skunk is 5.40 (Table 4, Figure 2).

p. 235, Table 2 and Results, 4th paragraph, vs p. 236, Table 3: the age-at-first-use cut-point changes. Age 15 is in the young group in Table 2 (15 or younger) but in the older group in Table 3 (<15 vs >=15).
